title: Light-dependent reactions; Respiration overview and glycolysis
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PS02b#t2 term and clue written for the game; PS02b#t3 term and clue written for the game; RS01#t3 term and clue written for the game; PS02b#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PS02b#N.2, RS01#N.2a, PS02b#N.5, RS01#N.9a, RS01#N.10, RS01#N.12b.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: P680
items.clue: Name of the reaction centre of the photosystem linked to water splitting.

items.label: P700
items.clue: Name of the reaction centre of the photosystem that passes electrons to NADP.

items.label: Pyruvate
items.clue: Product of the first stage; with oxygen available it enters the mitochondria.

items.label: Cyclic photophosphorylation
items.clue: An electron from PSI returns to PSI via the carriers: ATP only, no O₂, no reduced NADP.

questions.stem: Why is a structured array of many different pigment molecules, rather than a single chlorophyll molecule, needed to carry out the first step of photosynthesis?

options.text: Different pigments absorb a wide range of wavelengths and funnel the energy to one reaction centre, which is excited far more often than a lone molecule.
Each pigment molecule in the array carries out photosynthesis by itself, so the array simply packs more independent working units into the thylakoid membrane.
The accessory pigments only protect the chlorophyll from damage by bright light; a single chlorophyll could absorb the light equally well by itself.
Every pigment in the array emits its own excited electron to the electron carriers, so the array releases many more electrons per second than one molecule would.

questions.stem: Which organisms release energy by the oxidation of carbon compounds in cell respiration?

options.text: Heterotrophs at all times, but autotrophs only at night, when they cannot obtain energy from photosynthesis.
All autotrophs and all heterotrophs, in every living cell, throughout the day and the night.
Only organisms with lungs or gills, because respiration depends on breathing to take in oxygen from the air or water.
Heterotrophs and chemoautotrophs only, because photoautotrophs use light rather than oxidation as their energy source.

questions.explanation: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals all respire continuously. Photosynthesis in autotrophs is an extra process, not a replacement.

questions.stem: A herbicide blocks the flow of electrons out of photosystem II. Chloroplasts treated with it are kept in bright light with a supply of ADP, phosphate and NADP. Which process can continue?

options.text: Oxygen release, because light continues to split water molecules directly whether or not photosystem II passes on its electrons.
Continuous reduction of NADP, because photosystem I generates its own electrons from light and so needs no supply from elsewhere.
No ATP production at all, because both the cyclic and the non-cyclic pathways begin with electrons emitted by photosystem II.
ATP production by cyclic photophosphorylation, since photosystem I can still emit electrons that return to it via the carriers.

questions.stem: During glycolysis of one glucose molecule, two ATP are used in phosphorylation and four ATP are formed later. What is the net yield per glucose?

options.text: A net gain of 2 ATP together with 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 4 ATP as well as 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 6 ATP plus another 2 reduced NAD
A net gain of 2 ATP together with 2 oxidised NAD

questions.explanation: Four formed minus two used gives two ATP. The oxidation steps also give two reduced NAD, and two pyruvate form.

questions.stem: In one reaction of the Krebs cycle, two hydrogen atoms (each with an electron) are removed from a substrate and accepted by NAD. Which statement describes this reaction?

options.text: The substrate is reduced and NAD is oxidised by the transfer.
Neither substance is oxidised, because no oxygen takes part in it.
The substrate has been oxidised and NAD has been reduced.
The substrate is oxidised, but NAD only holds hydrogen and is unchanged.

questions.explanation: Removing hydrogen with its electron oxidises the substrate; NAD, which accepts it, is reduced. The two happen together as a redox reaction.

questions.stem: Aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule yields many times more ATP than anaerobic respiration (2). Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Both pathways run in the mitochondria, but without oxygen the mitochondria work more slowly and so make less ATP.
Without oxygen the cell uses the little oxygen dissolved in its cytoplasm, so only a small amount of ATP forms.
Without oxygen the cell converts glucose to ethanol, which keeps most of the energy, so much less ATP is made.
Without oxygen only glycolysis in the cytoplasm yields ATP; with oxygen the mitochondria release far more of the energy in glucose.
